analysis.one_liner: Caps US prescription drug prices at the average price charged in six other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, floor vote, or any cosponsor before the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a legal ceiling on the US list price of prescription drugs and biologics: no drug could be priced higher than the average list price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Drug makers would have to report their prices in those countries to the government each year, and a manufacturer selling above the cap would owe a penalty of ten times the overcharge for every unit sold. The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions for brand-name drugs and biologics, including people with high deductibles or no insurance who pay list-based prices, and insurers and employers who pay part of drug costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who buy brand-name prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Caps the US retail list price of every covered drug and biologic at the average list price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom, countries where the same medicines routinely sell for less. [S2] [S3]

Attaches a real penalty: a manufacturer that overcharges must pay ten times the difference between its US price and the international average, for every unit sold, giving companies a strong reason to comply. [S3]
Requires manufacturers to submit their own pricing data from those six countries annually, so the government can compute the cap without relying on estimates. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose US revenues from patented medicines would fall toward international price levels; if companies cut back on some drug development in response, future patients could see fewer new medicines.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps list prices, but many Americans with insurance pay based on negotiated prices and rebates rather than the list price, so the cap would not directly lower everyone's out-of-pocket cost at the pharmacy. [S2] [S3]
Brand-name manufacturers warn that reference-pricing policies reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines, and the bill offers no offsetting support for drug development. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Americans who pay high drug prices, especially the uninsured and underinsured, the cap is a large and direct benefit, and the penalty is set high enough to make evasion unattractive. The main honest cost is that lower drug revenues could mean somewhat less investment in future medicines, and the bill's focus on list prices means insured patients with heavy rebates would see smaller gains than its headline suggests. On balance the direct savings to consumers outweigh those costs, which is why the bill's fate rests on political choices rather than design flaws alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee in April 2023, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on April 19, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. [S1] [S5]
No other senator cosponsored the bill, so it never carried a second vote in the Senate. [S4]
The committee took no further action: no markup, no hearing on the bill, and no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off because the price cap never became law, leaving US list prices free to stay above the levels charged in comparable countries.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill and referred it to committee

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the life of the Congress without a markup, hearing, or vote.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of patented drugs and biologics
against.what_they_did: Opposed international reference-pricing proposals that would cap US drug prices at levels charged abroad.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so the record shows no partisan bloc ever took a position on it. [S4]

industries.note: The bill caps their US list prices at the average of six other wealthy countries and fines violators ten times the overcharge per unit, cutting directly into the highest-priced market in the world. Lower prices would mean lower revenue for the industry and lower costs for patients and payers.

industries.industry: Insurers and employers who pay drug bills
industries.note: A cap on list prices would lower the prices insurers and employers pay for brand-name drugs, savings that could flow back into premiums and benefits.
